newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-MOYA BLASTS INTO AUSTRALIAN OPEN FINAL 16.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-MOYA BLASTS INTO AUSTRALIAN OPEN FINAL 16.

text.p: Tournament heart-throb and giant-killer Carlos Moya of Spain blasted into the final 16 of the Australian Open on Friday, while Thailand's grand slam hopes were blown away in the women's singles.
Top seed Steffi Graf survived a brief scare for the second time in the tournament, but came from 1-4 down in the first set to beat Argentine Ines Gorrochategui 7-5 6-3.
Moya, who beat defending champion Boris Becker in a historic first-round upset, made short work of Germany's Bernd Karbacher, winning 6-2 6-2 6-2 before a big crowd of largely female fans.
His brow wrapped in a bandanna, Moya hardly seemed to raise a sweat as he disposed of Karbacher in just over an hour without offering the 59th ranked German a single break point.

The 20-year-old from the island of Majorca has taken over from American absentee Andre Agassi as the male pin-up of Melbourne Park. He will face Jonas Bjorkman of Sweden to extend his career-best grand slam performance here.

Fifth women's seed Anke Huber, so often playing in the shadow of fellow-German Graf, also swept into the final 16, beating Natasha Zvereva 7-5 6-0 to move a step closer to her second successive Open final.

"I am not playing as well as I did last year, not as consistent," said Huber, who has made slow starts in previous rounds and has been distracted by the mysterious collapse of her mother, Gerda, at the tournament this week.
"It's getting better each match and I hope I can still improve," Huber added.
Her mother was taken by ambulance to hospital after collapsing outside the players' lounge on Wednesday, and has since been given a clean bill of health.
Seventh seed Lindsay Davenport shattered Thailand's grand slam dreams in just 44 minutes on Friday to earn her fourth-round berth.

The American ended Tamarine Tanasugarn's brave run 6-1 6-0, but the Bangkok 19-year-old had already notched up Thailand's best-ever grand slam performance here by the time she reached up to shake the towering 1996 Olympic gold medallist by the hand.
"It's definitely my best match so far this year," Davenport told reporters. "I felt like I was hitting the ball really well."
World number one Graf again looked vulnerable. She struggled to find her range with her forehand early on, but came back to win 20 of 22 points to take the first set in 38 minutes.
Graf's campaign for a fifth Australian Open title has been eclipsed by the imminent verdict in her father, Peter's, trial on charges of evading tax on her earnings.
The verdict is expected hours before the women's singles final, but she has vowed to carry on.
Britain's grand slam hopes remained alive, with Tim Henman taking on world number two Michael Chang on a floodlit centre court on Friday night.

Henman, who has emerged one of Britain's most promising players since the great Fred Perry won three consecutive Wimbledons in the 1930s, was quoted by Australian bookmakers as a 9-4 chance to beat former French Open champion Chang.
